findings.title: An existing script fed to a shell on its standard input (cat land.sh | bash, bash < land.sh, bash -s < land.sh, sh < land.sh) is not read, so its merge or push to main passes: in a scheduled run and in an owner turn with no word.
findings.component: fixed/hooks/turngate.py parse_shell (shell reads its program from standard input: only echo/printf pipes and here-documents/here-strings are read; a `<` redirection from a file and `cat FILE |` are not)
findings.rule_quoted: D3: "Auto-merge, and a direct push to a default branch, need the same word as a merge. In a scheduled run they are always denied." / README: "A command is read through `bash -c`, `eval`, command substitution, a pipe or here-document into a shell, ... and these script files: | one handed to a shell (`bash FILE`, `sh FILE`) or to `source` / `.` | as a shell script"

findings.expected: deny[scheduled] in a scheduled run, and deny[merge-word] or deny[default-branch] with no word. `bash land.sh` (the control) is denied, and handing the same file to the same shell on standard input runs the same commands. The README names 'a pipe into a shell' among the routes it reads and does not list this form under 'What the gates cannot see'.
findings.how_it_arises: `cat script.sh | bash` and `bash < script.sh` are ordinary shell idioms. A script that holds a merge or a push to main (the repository keeps such helpers), run this way in a scheduled run, is not stopped. It goes through the same code path as the stated 'pipe into a shell' route, which reads only echo/printf and here-documents. Real row shapes (an ordinary Bash call). The same hole also covers a file the command itself writes and then pipes (DM-7).

findings.title: A GraphQL request body read from a file is judged as the file stands on disk before the command runs. When the same command first writes the merge mutation into that file (here-document, cp, echo >), the stale text is judged and the merge passes, also in a scheduled run. wget --post-file is not read at all.
findings.component: fixed/hooks/turngate.py _file_text / _gh_api body reading (rule E: request body from a file); HTTP programs other than curl
findings.rule_quoted: README: "A request body read from a file (`gh api -F key=@FILE`, ..., curl's `-d @FILE` ...) is read from the file ... and judged as if it were inline; a file that cannot be read keeps the verdict of a body the gate cannot see (a GraphQL call is denied as a merge whose target is unknown)" and "| one the same command text writes and then runs | what the text wrote"; D3 'always denied' in a scheduled run

findings.expected: deny (target-unknown / scheduled). The body the request sends is the mutation the same command wrote. A body file the command writes is not 'the file' as it is on disk at hook time, in the same way that a script the command writes is read as written. With no earlier file of that name the gate fails closed (control ctl-missing-file), so the hole opens exactly when a harmless file of the same name already exists.
findings.how_it_arises: A natural assistant pattern is to write a query to q.graphql, then later reuse the same file name for the mutation in one command (`cat > q.graphql <<EOF ... EOF; gh api graphql -F query=@q.graphql`). The first, harmless use leaves the file behind. Real row shapes. On the wget case: the README lists only gh and curl body flags. Inline wget --post-data with the mutation is denied (bbE.py E09) while --post-file passes.

findings.title: Honest orders are refused often: 11 of 30 plain orders are denied. Three examples stand out. "Let's merge #34." is refused because MERGE_NOUN_BEFORE reads "'s merge" as the noun, even though "let's" is listed in ORDER_LEADIN_WORDS. "Merge #34 and let me know when it's done." is refused. And these changes added two new refusals: "Next steps:\n- merge #34" and "Merge #34, then tell me what's next."
findings.component: fixed/hooks/turngate.py TYPED_ORDER/_is_verb (MERGE_NOUN_BEFORE `'s\s+$`), CONDITION_WORDS ('next', 'when', 'once', 'after') applied to the whole sentence (A1), list joining (A10)
findings.rule_quoted: decisions.md: "A false block is a defect too ... A gate that blocks honest work teaches the owner to ignore it." / README: "a typed order: the verb starts its clause (after words such as 'ok, please', 'go ahead and', 'can you')"; ORDER_LEADIN_WORDS includes "let's", "lets" (turngate.py:93-96); A10: "'Do these:\n- merge #34\n- upload the plugin': #34"

findings.expected: allow: each orders the merge (or push) now and names it. The stated cost is one card per refusal, and that is a defect when refusals are common (decisions: a false block teaches the owner to ignore the gate). A third of an ordinary sample is common. 'Let's merge #34' is refused although 'let's' is a listed lead-in, while 'Let's push to main' is accepted.
findings.how_it_arises: 'Let's merge #34' and 'merge it and let me know when it's done' are among the most ordinary orders an owner types, and a 'Next steps:' list is the usual way to give several. A1 reads a condition word anywhere in the sentence, so a report-back clause ('when it's done', 'once it's in', 'what's next') voids the order. Real row shapes. Mid-turn, the same report-back wording also ends a standing word under A6 ('Ping me when it's done.', bbA.py NB06/NB07). The README states the cost of the 'when you're done' form.

findings.title: 18 of 34 deliberate breaks of the new merge-gate rules leave every behavioural case of the fix's 950-case table passing, although each break changes a verdict. CPU times were measured in process because the machine was shared; wall times are higher.
